say: You give it an equation with the unknown in the **power**, like $a^{x} = b$. It finds $x$.
The key idea: taking a log of both sides lets the log law $\ln a^{x} = x \ln a$ bring the exponent down to ground level, where you can solve for it.

how.higher: It is a part of its own on Paper 1 in most years from 2016, worth 5 to 10 marks, and a step inside longer modelling questions on decay, cooling and growth, where you solve for the time.

example.question: A town's population is modelled by $P(t) = 200(1.05)^{t}$, where $t$ is the time in years. Find, correct to one decimal place, when the population reaches $500$.

steps.title: Isolate the power
steps.say: Put $P = 500$. Then get the power $1.05^{\hl{1}{t}}$ on its own by dividing both sides by $200$.

steps.title: Take logs
steps.say: Take $\ln$ of both sides. The log law brings the exponent $\hl{1}{t}$ down in front.

lines.text: Any base works. Use the same log on both sides.

steps.title: Solve for t
steps.say: Divide both sides by $\ln 1.05$. Then use the calculator and round.

higher.tip: Get the power on its own before you take logs. The marks are tied to that first step.
You can take logs to any base, so use $\ln$ or $\log_{10}$, whichever you like.
Handle the logs correctly. An equation in $t$ with no indices, logs done properly, earns high partial credit.
Round as the question asks. A wrong or missing rounding costs one mark off full credit.

sources.quote: Apply a * for answer not rounded

say: You give it an equation with $a^{2x}$, $a^{x}$ and a number, like $a^{2x} + b\,a^{x} + c = 0$. It finds $x$.
The key idea: $a^{2x} = (a^{x})^{2}$, so call $a^{x}$ by one letter and the equation is an ordinary **quadratic**. Solve it, then turn each answer back into $x$.

how.higher: It is a 10-mark part on Paper 1 (2016, 2021 and 2022), usually straight after a part that sets up or solves a similar quadratic, so you reuse that method with $a^{x}$ in place of $x$.

steps.title: See the quadratic
steps.say: Write $3^{2x}$ as $(3^{x})^{2}$. Now the equation is a quadratic in $\hl{1}{3^{x}}$.

steps.title: Use a new letter
steps.say: Let $\hl{1}{y} = \hl{1}{3^{x}}$. It is easier to factorise with a plain letter.

steps.title: Solve for y
steps.say: Each bracket gives a value of $\hl{1}{y}$.

steps.title: Go back to x
steps.say: Replace $\hl{1}{y}$ with $3^{x}$. A power of $3$ is never negative, so $3^{x} = -9$ has no solution. Cross it out.

higher.tip: Turn the equation into a quadratic first. Some work in writing it that way earns low partial credit.

sources.quote: Some work in writing given equation

higher.tip: Rule out the negative value of $a^{x}$ and say why. Leaving it in loses a mark.
Treat it as a quadratic. Simplifying it some other way earns low partial credit at most.
When both roots are valid, turn both back into $x$. Finding only one loses a mark.

say: You give it the sum formula for a geometric series, $a + ar + \cdots + ar^{n-1} = \frac{a(1 - r^{n})}{1 - r}$. It **proves** it is true for every $n \ge 1$.
Induction is a line of dominoes. Show the first one falls. Then show that any one falling knocks the next. For a sum, the next sum is the last sum plus one new term.

example.question: Prove by induction that $5 + 15 + 45 + \cdots + 5(3^{n-1}) = \frac{5(3^{n} - 1)}{2}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

steps.title: Check n = 1
steps.say: Test the formula for $n = 1$. The sum has one term.

lines.text: They match, so it is true for $n = 1$.

steps.title: Assume true for k
steps.say: Assume the formula is true for $n = k$. You will use it in the next step.

steps.title: Prove for k + 1
steps.say: Take $n = k + 1$. The sum is the sum to $k$ terms plus the next term, $5(3^{k})$. Replace the sum to $k$ terms with $\hl{1}{\frac{5(3^{k} - 1)}{2}}$.

lines.text: To prove: the sum to $k + 1$ terms is $\frac{5(3^{k+1} - 1)}{2}$.

steps.title: Write the conclusion
steps.say: State all three parts of the conclusion.

lines.text: True for $n = 1$. If true for $n = k$, then true for $n = k + 1$. So true for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

say: You give it a claim that a number $d$ divides an expression in $n$, like "$3$ divides $4^{n} + 2$". It **proves** it for every $n \ge 1$.
The key idea: assume it for $n = k$ by writing the expression as a multiple of $d$. Then rebuild the $n = k + 1$ expression out of that multiple and take out a factor of $d$.

how.higher: It is a 15-mark part on Paper 1 (2016 and 2021, both Question 4(a)), where the statement is given and you prove it by induction.

example.question: Prove by induction that $4^{n} + 2$ is divisible by $3$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

steps.title: Check n = 1
steps.say: Test $n = 1$. Show the answer is a multiple of $3$.

lines.text: It is divisible by $3$, so it is true for $n = 1$.

steps.title: Assume true for k
steps.say: Assume it is true for $n = k$. Write the expression as $3$ times a whole number $M$, then rearrange for $4^{k}$.

steps.title: Prove for k + 1
steps.say: Take $n = k + 1$. Split off one factor of $4$, so $4^{k}$ appears. Replace $4^{k}$ with $\hl{1}{3M - 2}$.

lines.text: This is $3$ times a whole number, so $4^{k+1} + 2$ is divisible by $3$.

steps.title: Write the conclusion
steps.say: State all three parts of the conclusion.

lines.text: True for $n = 1$. If true for $n = k$, then true for $n = k + 1$. So true for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

higher.tip: Each of the three steps earns marks: $P(1)$, the assumption $P(k)$ and $P(k+1)$. They can be in any order.
The higher marks come from using $P(k)$ to prove $P(k+1)$. Writing out the steps is not enough.
